documents.unit: Faculty of Arts and Sciences, Office of Undergraduate Education (Harvard College)
documents.title: Generative AI Guidance
documents.summary: The FAS Office of Undergraduate Education requires every faculty member to tell students the course AI policy and offers three sample policies from banning to encouraging. It also advises against AI detectors, sets privacy limits, and announces a lockdown exam browser.
documents.stance_why: It says "All faculty are required to inform students of the policies" and lets faculty "choose from among the below example policies" from "maximally restrictive" to "fully-encouraging", so the college sets no stance itself and hands the decision to instructors with tiered templates.

units.why: The page opens with "Harvard supports responsible experimentation with generative AI tools" and names risks; a general statement of purpose and principles, so P56, not a specific rule.
units.anchor: Harvard supports responsible experimentation with generative AI tools

units.why: Respondus is offered "to ensure that students do not use AI unless the course asks them to do so" in "in-person seated exams and quizzes". It is about exam conditions, so P22.
units.anchor: Respondus, a new browser lockdown tool
units.policy: Faculty can use the Respondus browser lockdown tool on Canvas for in-person seated exams and quizzes to ensure that students do not use AI unless the course asks them to do so.

units.why: "All faculty are required to inform students of the policies" is a mandate on instructors to state an AI policy, which is P09.
units.anchor: All faculty are required to inform students of the policies governing generative AI use

units.why: "Whether students ... are forbidden ... or expected to explore its limits" shows the stance is left to each course. P04 fits; the clarity point is secondary.
units.anchor: Whether students in your course are forbidden from using ChatGPT or expected to explore its
units.policy: Whether students are forbidden from using ChatGPT or expected to explore its limits is set by the course's policy, which makes expectations clear to students.

units.why: "you should post your policy on your Canvas site" tells instructors where to communicate the policy; closest type is P09 (state the policy to students).
units.anchor: you should post your policy on your Canvas site

units.why: Faculty may "choose from among the below example policies ... or design your own". The menu is a set of named templates (restrictive, fully encouraging, mixed), so P05 rather than P04, since the options are explicitly sorted.
units.anchor: choose from among the below example policies to add to your Canvas site, or you
units.policy: Faculty may choose from the example policies (maximally restrictive, fully encouraging, mixed) or design their own to suit the course.

units.why: The maximally restrictive draft says "We specifically forbid the use of ChatGPT or any other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools at all stages", a ban on all work: P01.
units.anchor: We specifically forbid the use of ChatGPT or any other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools
units.policy: In the maximally restrictive sample policy, ChatGPT or any other generative AI tools are forbidden at all stages of the work process, including preliminary ones.

units.why: "all work students submit for this course will be their own" requires submitted work to be the student's own: P29.
units.anchor: all work students submit for this course will be their own

units.why: Group work "list all team members who participated" is an attribution rule for collaboration. It is not about AI directly; P29 (submitted work is truthfully the students') fits best.
units.anchor: we expect for the assignment to list all team members who participated

units.why: "Violations of this policy will be considered academic misconduct" classifies prohibited AI use as misconduct: P36. Later identical sentences in the other templates are not recoded.
units.anchor: Violations of this policy will be considered academic misconduct

units.why: "different classes at Harvard could implement different AI policies, and it is the student's responsibility to conform" says one course's rule does not carry over to others: P11.
units.anchor: different classes at Harvard could implement different AI policies
units.policy: Different classes at Harvard could implement different AI policies, and it is the student's responsibility to conform to expectations for each course.

units.why: The fully-encouraging draft "encourages students to explore" AI "for all assignments and assessments": default encourage, P02.
units.anchor: This course encourages students to explore the use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) tools

units.why: "Any such use must be appropriately acknowledged and cited" requires acknowledgment with the submission: P24. The same sentence in the mixed draft is not recoded.
units.anchor: Any such use must be appropriately acknowledged and cited

units.why: Students must "assess the validity and applicability of any GAI output" and "bear the final responsibility". Both verification (P31) and ownership (P29) fit; P31 chosen because the sentence is about assessing validity.
units.anchor: responsibility to assess the validity and applicability of any GAI output that is submitted
units.policy: Each student is responsible for assessing the validity and applicability of any GAI output that is submitted and bears the final responsibility.

units.why: The mixed draft says "The default is that such use is disallowed unless otherwise stated", a fallback rule for assignments that do not say: P06.
units.anchor: The default is that such use is disallowed unless otherwise stated

units.why: "Certain assignments ... will permit or even encourage" AI describes permission set assignment by assignment; P04 fits (the default is P06, coded separately).
units.anchor: Certain assignments in this course will permit or even encourage the use of generative artificial

units.why: The Bok Center link offers "resources on teaching in the age of AI" including course and assessment design; support for faculty learning about AI: P63.
units.anchor: Visit the Bok Center for Teaching and Learning website for resources on teaching in the

units.why: Faculty sessions shared "advice on how to AI-proof familiar assignments"; this is faculty support and learning, P63, not a rule.
units.anchor: advice on how to “AI-proof” familiar assignments

units.why: "some of the material they provide as factual are incorrect" warns that AI output can be wrong: P31.
units.anchor: some of the material they provide as factual are incorrect

units.why: "will reflect the biases and inaccuracies that are contained in the training data" names bias as a weakness of AI. P53 (bias) fits as the sentence is about bias; hallucination is a separate sentence.
units.anchor: the GAI responses will reflect the biases and inaccuracies that are contained in the training

units.why: "We should assume that all our students are proficient with these tools and should adjust our expectations accordingly" tells instructors to redesign around AI: P35.
units.anchor: We should assume that all our students are proficient with these tools and should adjust

units.why: The challenge is "to incentivize the level of engagement that leads to a deeper understanding"; a rationale that learning needs engagement, closest to P41.
units.anchor: incentivize the level of engagement that leads to a deeper understanding

units.why: "feed representative assignments ... into a GAI tool" recommends testing assignments against AI when designing a course: P35.
units.anchor: feed representative assignments from your upcoming courses into a GAI tool such as ChatGPT

units.why: "decide on and disseminate a course-by-course policy" puts the decision with each course: P04.
units.anchor: decide on and disseminate a course-by-course policy on student use of GAI tools

units.why: "We also need to teach our students how to use these tools in an ethical and responsible manner" says courses should teach AI use: P44.
units.anchor: We also need to teach our students how to use these tools in an ethical

units.why: "It would be inadvisable to count on automated methods for GAI detection" advises against relying on detectors: P39.
units.anchor: It would be inadvisable to count on automated methods for GAI detection

units.why: "FAS does not plan to provide/license such a tool" states that no AI-detection tool will be supplied; it is about institutional provision, and P39 ("will not be used or relied upon") fits closest.
units.anchor: FAS does not plan to provide/license such a tool for use in courses

units.why: FAS "does not plan to provide/license" an internet-blocking proctoring tool. This is an institutional tooling decision about exams, not a rule for students or a detector statement, so no type fits: UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: exam proctoring that aim to block students from using the internet
units.uncovered_note: FAS states it will not provide or license internet-blocking exam proctoring technology for course use.

units.why: "No confidential information can be loaded into GAI systems" is a data privacy rule: P50.
units.anchor: No confidential information can be loaded into GAI systems

units.why: "Faculty must get documented permission from students before putting original student content into any generative AI tool" protects student data: P50, not P59, since it limits rather than describes teaching uses.
units.anchor: Faculty must get documented permission from students before putting original student content into any generative

units.why: "terms of service allow the company to access any information fed into it" warns that tools keep what is entered: P50.
units.anchor: terms of service allow the company to access any information fed into it

units.why: "Harvard HUIT has compiled a list of available tools" points users to university-vetted tools: P50 (prefer vetted tools).
units.anchor: Harvard HUIT has compiled a list of available tools

documents.title: Teach with Generative AI
documents.summary: The university AI site is a faculty-facing resource that encourages experimenting with GenAI in teaching and gives assessment redesign, risk and privacy advice. It states that schools let individual instructors customize AI policies if clearly communicated.
documents.stance_why: It says "Schools within Harvard allow for the customization of AI usage policies by individual instructors, provided these are clearly communicated", so the page sets no student-facing rule itself and delegates.

units.why: "Harvard has consistently tried to embrace new technology" frames the institution's welcoming posture toward GenAI: P56 (institution-level framing).
units.anchor: Harvard has consistently tried to embrace new technology across our classrooms

units.why: Tools are "free and open to all faculty, students and staff behind Harvard Key"; the university provides sanctioned tools: P17.
units.anchor: free and open to all faculty, students and staff behind Harvard Key

units.why: Concerns that GenAI may "promote academic dishonesty, and facilitate lazy learning" give a reason to limit AI: P41.
units.anchor: promote academic dishonesty, and facilitate “lazy learning.”

units.why: Faculty want "to understand how GenAI tools can enhance the educational experience", a rationale for using AI in teaching; P44 is the closest type.
units.anchor: how GenAI tools can enhance the educational experience and build more vibrant classrooms

units.why: "it's essential to learn (and perhaps teach) how to write a prompt that works" treats prompting as a skill to teach: P44.
units.anchor: it’s essential to learn (and perhaps teach) how to write a prompt that works

units.why: Errors arise "because LLMs are fundamentally probabilistic": an output reliability caution, P31.
units.anchor: because LLMs are fundamentally probabilistic

units.why: Faculty used LLMs for "producing course materials, personalizing feedback, generating assignments": instructor teaching uses, P59.
units.anchor: Many faculty used LLMs to improve different (and sometimes mundane) aspects

units.why: "GenAI can assist with overcoming these skill gaps: coding for a business class" welcomes AI use by students to get past barriers: P02.
units.anchor: GenAI can assist with overcoming these skill gaps

units.why: "a tutor bot that answered questions like course staff" is an example of a course-specific AI tutor: P17.
units.anchor: created a tutor bot that answered questions like course staff

units.why: "algorithmic biases, digital divides, and fake content" names harms of LLMs: P53.
units.anchor: algorithmic biases, digital divides, and fake content

units.why: "this page will be updated frequently" commits to revising the guidance as the technology changes: P54.
units.anchor: this page will be updated frequently with new resources and advice

units.why: "AI can help you outline your course, create learning objectives, and suggest assignments" advises instructors on AI in course prep: P59.
units.anchor: AI can help you outline your course, create learning objectives, and suggest assignments

units.why: "AI tools can help write, modify, or create question sets" and rubrics: instructor use for assessment materials, P59.
units.anchor: how AI tools can help write, modify, or create question sets

units.why: GenAI can "generate summaries of relevant readings", "brand new cases" and slideshow content: instructor use for course content, P59.
units.anchor: generate summaries of relevant readings or videos you might want to include for students

units.why: Instructors can "make a personal tutorbot" from the syllabus and lectures: a course-specific AI tool, P17; practice problems are incidental.
units.anchor: help make a personal tutorbot, generate unlimited practice problems

units.why: "LLMs can be used to provide initial personalized feedback to your students" is instructor AI use for feedback, P59, not P46 because it is initial feedback rather than grading.
units.anchor: LLMs can be used to provide initial personalized feedback to your students

units.why: "creating assessments that emphasize skills where AI tools fall short" tells instructors to redesign assessment around AI: P35.
units.anchor: creating assessments that emphasize skills where AI tools fall short

units.why: "Design tasks and assessments that require creativity, practical application ... and critical thinking" is assignment redesign: P35.
units.anchor: Design tasks and assessments that require creativity, practical application of concepts, and critical thinking

units.why: "test intermediate steps in the learning process, instead of just the final product" is process-based assessment redesign: P35.
units.anchor: test intermediate steps in the learning process, instead of just the final product

units.why: "at a minimum provide clear guidelines about the use of AI-generated content" asks instructors to state AI expectations in assignments: P09.
units.anchor: at a minimum provide clear guidelines about the use of AI-generated content in assignments and

units.why: "entirely made-up answers" (hallucinations) that may not be eliminated: an output reliability warning, P31.
units.anchor: yielding garbled or entirely made-up answers

units.why: "Good AI use involves being aware of, checking for, and making efforts to correct such biases" names bias and asks users to check for it: P53.
units.anchor: Good AI use involves being aware of, checking for, and making efforts to correct such

units.why: "Personal data is not supposed to be fed to GenAI models" is a data protection rule: P50.
units.anchor: Personal data is not supposed to be fed to GenAI models

units.why: "you should shift the kind of assignments you are providing students ... as well as enforce academic dishonesty policies" combines redesign and enforcement; redesign (P35) is the main directive and enforcement is not given separately.
units.anchor: you should shift the kind of assignments you are providing students

units.why: "AI-tutored students performed as well or better" cites a study on AI and learning outcomes: P55.
units.anchor: AI-tutored students performed as well or better

units.why: "the best place is to start is the Harvard AI Sandbox" recommends a sanctioned university tool: P17.
units.anchor: the best place is to start is the Harvard AI Sandbox

units.why: "other existing policies ... also apply to GenAI" sets the scope of existing rules (security, accessibility, IP): P56.
units.anchor: other existing policies, such as Harvard’s Information Security Policy

units.why: "be aware of the University's guidelines ... and to refer to School-specific policies" points instructors to institutional guidance: P56.
units.anchor: be aware of the University’s guidelines designed to ensure responsible and effective use of these

units.why: "must align with the principles of honesty, respect, and responsibility, ensuring that students' work remains original" states principle and requires original work: P29.
units.anchor: ensuring that students’ work remains original and reflective of their understanding and skills

units.why: "Schools within Harvard allow for the customization of AI usage policies by individual instructors" delegates the stance to instructors: P04.
units.anchor: allow for the customization of AI usage policies by individual instructors

units.why: "students and faculty are encouraged to be transparent about the use of generative AI" with "proper attribution": encourages disclosure, P24.
units.anchor: students and faculty are encouraged to be transparent about the use of generative AI in

units.anchor: Consider co-creating course-specific norms around the use of generative AI with your students

units.why: "we encourage you to engage with peers and organizations at Harvard" supports faculty learning about AI: P63.
units.anchor: we encourage you to engage with peers and organizations at Harvard

documents.unit: John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Computing in Engineering Education
documents.title: Generative AI
documents.summary: A short SEAS service page in which the Computing in Engineering Education team offers to support faculty integrating generative AI into computational courses and links to Harvard integrity standards. It sets no student rules.
documents.stance_why: The page only commits to "supporting faculty and staff in the effective and responsible integration of Generative AI" and links to university guidance; it states no rule on student AI use, so it delegates.

units.why: "committed to supporting faculty and staff in the effective and responsible integration of Generative AI" is a support commitment for faculty: P63.
units.anchor: committed to supporting faculty and staff in the effective and responsible integration of Generative AI

units.why: "believe that it can enhance the computational learning environment" is a rationale that welcomes AI: P44.
units.anchor: believe that it can enhance the computational learning environment at SEAS

units.why: "Interested faculty and staff should contact CEE to request a consultation" offers consultations to faculty: P63.
units.anchor: Interested faculty and staff should contact CEE to request a consultation

units.why: Links are provided "to ensure that students and faculty adhere to Harvard academic integrity standards"; it points to standards without stating a rule: P56.
units.anchor: students and faculty adhere to Harvard academic integrity standards and best practices

units.why: The link list names "OpenAI ChatGPT Edu for Harvard" and "AI Sandbox" as tools available from HUIT: university-provided tools, P17.
units.anchor: G-AI Tools Available from HUIT

notes: Coder A. Provost, HUIT and FAS university guideline pages were inaccessible (Access Denied), so only the three included documents were coded. No computing-unit or course documents. One UNCOVERED unit (FAS will not license exam-proctoring internet-blocking tools). Repeated template sentences (misconduct, acknowledge-and-cite, student validity duty) were coded once per document.
